analysis.one_liner: Requires flammable liquid storage terminals to install overflow alarms with federal inspections and daily fines.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with zero cosponsors, it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and sent to its Health and Safety Subcommittee, where it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every terminal that stores flammable liquids to have a high-level alarm that sounds before a tank overflows. New alarm plans would need federal approval and inspection, workers would have to be trained, unattended facilities would need systems that can automatically shut off fuel flow, and owners would owe a $5,000 fine per violation per day. It was meant to prevent tank overfill fires, spills, and explosions.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and people who live or work near fuel storage terminals, who face fire, explosion, and toxic spill risk when a tank is overfilled. Terminal workers get alarms audible across the facility, training in written procedures, and automatic shutoffs at unattended sites.

how_it_helps.text: Every terminal storing flammable liquids must install a high-level alarm set to trigger before a tank overflows, accounting for filling rate and shutdown time [S2][S3].

At unattended terminals, the alarm system must be able to shut off or divert the liquid flow on danger of overfilling, even during a power failure, so no overfill depends on a person being present [S3].
Plans and specifications must be approved by OSHA before installation, and OSHA must inspect each new system for compliance [S2][S3].
Terminal workers must be trained under written procedures for overfill prevention, and alarms must give a distinctive sound for overfill danger, power loss, circuit faults, and malfunctions [S2][S3].
Owners must file fire and emergency plans with the local fire department and face a $5,000 civil penalty per violation per day, enforced by the Attorney General in federal court [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of fuel and flammable-liquid storage terminals, who would pay for alarm installation, quarterly testing and recordkeeping, training, and federal plan approvals, and up to $5,000 per violation per day if they do not comply.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes real costs on terminal owners: buying and installing approved alarm systems, quarterly testing with records kept for inspection, worker training, and federal plan approval before installation, plus penalties of $5,000 per violation per day [S2][S3].

The requirement that OSHA approve plans and specifications and inspect every installation adds a federal review step before any new alarm can go in, which terminal owners and some legislators would see as slow, costly federal micromanagement of what is already covered by fire codes [S3].
The bill is a one-industry mandate that was introduced with no cosponsors, so it never had a coalition behind it that could negotiate the design or the compliance deadlines [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefit is straightforward: automatic alarms and shutoffs prevent tank overfills, which cause fires, explosions, and fuel spills that harm workers and neighbors. The compliance cost falls on a narrow set of storage terminal owners, and existing alarm systems that can be shown to work are grandfathered in [S3]. The main design weakness is the added OSHA plan-approval and inspection layer, which duplicates work that fire codes and NFPA-approved equipment already cover. On balance the public-safety gain is real and the cost is concentrated on the facilities that create the risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, which passed it along to the Health and Safety Subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Frank Guarini introduced the bill on January 31, 1989; no other member cosponsored it [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
On February 21, 1989, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Health and Safety, where no further action is recorded [S5].
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill died in subcommittee without a hearing, a vote, or floor action [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Terminal owners and operators of flammable liquid storage facilities are better off, because they avoided alarm installation, testing, training, and federal inspection costs and the $5,000-per-day penalty that the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Rep. Frank J. Guarini
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring overflow alarms at flammable liquid terminals and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor — Subcommittee on Health and Safety
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 21, 1989 and took no recorded action; the bill died in subcommittee without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: There was no recorded opposition or vote; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors, so no party position is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Fuel and flammable liquid storage terminals (petroleum and chemical bulk storage)
industries.note: The bill would make terminal owners pay for alarms, quarterly testing, worker training, fire plans, federal plan approvals, and up to $5,000 per violation per day. Its safety value comes directly at those owners' expense, and with the bill's death they avoided the entire cost.
Terminal operators would have had to buy NFPA-approved high-level alarm systems, creating a market for safety equipment makers.
